previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Thompson was admitted with acute gastrointestinal bleeding and heart failure exacerbation, presenting with melena, hypotension, and dyspnea. He had a history of recurrent GI bleeding on anticoagulation for a mechanical aortic valve. Warfarin was held and heparin bridged due to high stroke risk. He received multiple blood transfusions for hemoglobin dropping to 6.6 g/dL. Endoscopy and capsule study identified gastric and small bowel angiodysplasias as the likely source, with colonoscopy showing diverticulosis but no active bleeding. He was managed conservatively with pantoprazole, sucralfate, and iron supplementation. Heart failure was treated with IV diuresis, transitioning to oral torsemide, with improvement in volume status and weight reduction to 78 kg. A PICC line was placed for ongoing transfusion access. Warfarin was restarted at a lower target INR of 2.0–3.0. He was discharged home with services, on a plan for weekly pheresis unit transfusions, close INR and hemoglobin monitoring, and follow-up with cardiology and gastroenterology for possible APC therapy.
problems: Unspecified gastritis and gastroduodenitis, with hemorrhage
Acute on chronic combined systolic and diastolic heart failure
Angiodysplasia of stomach and duodenum without mention of hemorrhage
Diverticulosis of colon (without mention of hemorrhage)
Iron deficiency anemia secondary to blood loss (chronic)
Heart valve replaced by other means
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled

Brief Hospital Course:
___ year old man with coronary artery disease and stenting in the 
distal LAD, mechanical AVR, and CVA x4 on warfarin complicated 
by frequent hemorrhagic gastritis (also has known gastric AVM 
and colon diverticulosis) who presented to the ED with 
hypotension during outpatient regular blood transfusion. He was 
at high risk for GI bleeding given his history and 
anticoagulation with warfarin despite decreased therapeutic goal 
to INR = ___. His most likely source of bleeding was from upper 
GI tract given his history of hemorrhagic gastritis and gastric 
AVM. He had a recent colonoscopy in ___ that showed 
diverticulosis, which can also potentially bleed. His INR was 
2.6 on admission. He was treated with pantoprazole IV then PO.  
From ___ to ___, he received a total of 7 units of PRBC 
transfusion for continually dropping hematocrit.  After much 
discussion with GI, Cardiology, and the patient, the decision 
was made to pursue EGD with possible use of argon-plasma 
coagulator.  Coumadin stopped and INR allowed to drift down to 
1.5.  EGD performed on ___ revealing angioectasia.  
Argon-plasma coagulator treatment was applied.  Heparin gtt 
started after the EGD and Coumadin started the day after the 
procedure.  For the 72 hours following the procedure, the 
patient's HCT remained stable even while the PTT was in or above 
the therapeutic range.  Dr. ___ patient's cardiologist 
said it was okay to stop heparin once the INR was close to the 
therapeutic range.  Specifically, INR 1.6 was okay for heparin 
to be stopped.  The reason is that clot formation on a 
prosthetic valve in the aortic position is relatively low.  The 
patient was discharged home with slightly subtherapeutic INR 
with instructions to continue taking warfarin only for 
anticoagulation.

The patient does have borderline hypotension and SBP in the 
outpatient setting is usually 100-120. He was initially 
euvolemic on exam but CXR showed some edema and bilateral 
pleural effusions. We continued on atorvastatin but initially 
held metoprolol and diuretics in the setting of borderline 
hypotension. He then developed some dyspnea and chest pain. 
Repeat EKG showed old unchanged posterior, inferior and lateral 
q waves and cardiac enzymes were normal. Repeat CXR showed 
increased moderate bilateral pleural effusions with persistent 
mild pulmonary edema. Extra doses of Lasix were used. He was 
then restarted on his home dose of torsemide.  He continued to 
have edema but was not actively diuresed until after his 
bleeding was controlled.

He is off aspirin but can restart if chest pain. However, 
currently the patient's more acute and life threatening probelm 
is bleeding, and he is already on coumadin for his aortic valve, 
which should offer some but not ideal protection against 
recurrent MI.  He then developed shoulder pain consistent with 
calcific tendenitis/capsulitis. He had severe tenderness and an 
X ray confirmed calcific tendonitis.  He was seen by orthopedics 
who stated this was either tendonitis or arthritis and he was 
developing frozen shoulder so he was treated with steroid 
injection which over time in conjunction w/ po oxycodone 
improved his symptoms. He should follow up in shoulder clinic in

CHEST RADIOGRAPH PERFORMED ON ___.

CLINICAL HISTORY:  ___ man with crackles at the left lung base, assess

FINDINGS:  AP upright and lateral views of the chest were obtained.  AICD

Small bilateral layering effusions are also noted.

IMPRESSION:  Cardiomegaly with bilateral pleural effusions and mild pulmonary
edema.  PICC line tip appears to be located within the cavoatrial junction.

INDICATION:  ___ male with GI bleeding, history of heart failure with
coronary stents and acute dyspnea and chest pain.  Evaluate for pulmonary
edema from blood transfusions.

COMPARISON:  ___.

CHEST, AP UPRIGHT AND LATERAL VIEWS:  AICD device in the left chest wall is
unchanged with two leads following a normal course terminating in the expected
region of the right atrium and right ventricle.  Sternotomy wires are intact. 
There are increased moderate bilateral pleural effusions.  Mild interstitial
prominence is similar to prior, without overt edema.  Cardiomediastinal
silhouette is stable.  Left PICC has been removed.

IMPRESSION:  Increased moderate bilateral pleural effusions with persistent
mild pulmonary edema.

LEFT SHOULDER STUDY DATED ___

No prior studies for comparison.

FINDINGS:  A cluster of calcifications is present in the region of the left
rotator cuff in keeping with clinically suspected calcific tendinitis.  No
acute fracture or dislocation is identified.  Apparent high riding left
shoulder could reflect chronic rotator cuff degeneration or may in part be
projectional.  Degenerative changes are present at the left acromioclavicular
joint with joint space narrowing in this region.

IMPRESSION:  Clustered periarticular calcifications in keeping with clinically
suspected calcific tendinitis.

INDICATION:  ___ male on anticoagulation with somnolence and confusion
and history of stroke.  Evaluate for intracranial hemorrhage.

COMPARISON:  ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Axial CT images through the head were acquired without intravenous
contrast.  Initial acquisition was partially degraded by motion artifact. 
Subsequent repeat partial acquisition was improved.

FINDINGS:  There is no evidence for acute intracranial hemorrhage, mass
effect, edema, or hydrocephalus.  There is preservation of gray-white
differentiation without evidence for an acute major vascular territorial
infarct.  Small bifrontal chronic infarcts are unchanged.  White matter
hypodensities, left greater than right, are likely secondary to sequela of
chronic small vessel infarcts.  A subcentimeter hypodensity is again seen in
the left cerebellar hemisphere, consistent with a chronic infarct.  Mild
ventricular and sulcal prominence suggests age-related involutional changes. 
Vertebro-basilar dolichoectasia and calcified plaque are again noted.  Carotid
artery calcifications are also again seen.  Visualized bones and soft tissues
are grossly unremarkable.  

Mild mucosal thickening in the anterior ethmoid air cells is again seen.

IMPRESSION:  No acute intracranial hemorrhage and no CT evidence of an acute
major vascular territorial infarction.  MRI would be more sensitive for an
acute infarction, if clinically warranted.
